models.collectorNote: The DS is rolling sculpture with an engineering degree, and the market treats early, correct cars that way. Hydraulics want specialists and regular use; the Chapron convertibles and the DS 23 Injection sit at the top of the range.

generations.name: DS 19
generations.note: The original car paired a modest 1.9 litre engine and 75 hp with Paul Magès' high-pressure hydraulics, which levelled the suspension, powered the brakes, steering and semi-automatic clutch, and let the driver raise the car for rough roads. It was the first mass-produced car with disc brakes.

generations.name: DS 20, DS 21 and DS 23
generations.note: Engines grew through 2.0 and 2.2 litres to the 2.3 litre DS 23, whose fuel-injected version made 130 hp DIN, the most powerful production DS. The 1967 restyle added headlights that swivelled with the steering, behind glass, years before regulations elsewhere allowed them.

models.intro: Paris, October 1955: the DS landed like a spacecraft among cars that still had running boards. Hydropneumatic suspension, powered brakes and steering, disc brakes, a body by sculptor Flaminio Bertoni. By the end of the first day, Citroën had taken 12,000 orders. Production ran twenty years and 1,455,746 cars.

models.collectorNote: France's Beetle, with the same rule: buy the best body you can find, because rust, not mechanics, is the enemy. Early ripple-bonnet cars and Charlestons lead the market; the twin-engine Sahara 4x4 is the unicorn.

generations.name: Early cars (375 and 425 cc)
generations.note: Pierre Boulanger's TPV prototypes were hidden from the occupying forces during the war. The production car launched in 1948 with a 375 cc flat-twin and 9 hp, corrugated panels, a full-length canvas roof and suspension soft enough to cross a field at speed.

generations.name: 602 cc cars
generations.note: The 602 cc engine peaked at 33 hp in 1970 and settled at 29 hp for the final cars, which gained the Charleston's two-tone paint as a regular model. The last 2CV left Mangualde in Portugal on 27 July 1990, ending one of the longest production runs in history.

models.intro: The brief was an umbrella on four wheels: carry two farmers and 100 kilos of goods at 60 km/h across a ploughed field without breaking the eggs in the basket. The 2CV answered it for 42 years, selling 3,872,583 saloons and over a million vans with almost no change.
